food.text: Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan described a rich produce supply in the Khmer Empire in the late 13th century. Vegetables included onions, mustard, chives, eggplants, watermelons and winter gourds. Fruits included pomegranates, sugarcane, lotus roots, bananas, lychees and oranges.
Between the 9th and 15th century, the growing Khmer Empire's culinary influence spread beyond the borders of modern-day Cambodia. It reached what is now Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Indonesia.

Trade between China and the Indonesian archipelago flourished from the era of Srivijaya around the 10th century and intensified in the Majapahit era around the 15th century. Chinese immigrants began to settle in the archipelago, bringing their culture and cuisine. This laid the ground for Southeast Asian adaptations of Chinese fried rice, such as nasi goreng.

According to Zhou Daguan, five fermented alcoholic beverages were produced in the late-13th century Khmer Empire. One of them was mead, the honey-based drink, and the others were made from leaves, rice leftovers, sugar and palm starch.

Archaeobotanical investigations at 14th to 15th century Angkor Thom found macroremains of rice, sesame, mung beans, pigeon peas, hyacinth beans and yardlong beans. These traces of plant food show what was grown and eaten in the late Khmer Empire.

Food crops were actively cultivated in tropical gardens in and around the cities and temples of the Khmer Empire. Archaeobotanical work at Angkor Wat and Ta Prohm identified rice, sesame, mung beans, crepe ginger, black peppers and long peppers, as well as citron or kaffir lime rind.

It is unclear when people in present-day Indonesia began cooking fried rice. Chinese people usually favor freshly cooked hot food, and it is taboo in their culture to throw away uneaten food, so the previous day's leftover rice was often recooked in the morning. Gregory Rodgers suggested that frying the rice could prevent the propagation of dangerous microbes, especially with pre-refrigeration technology in Indonesia, and also avoid the need to throw out precious food.

Two of the five fermented drinks of the late-13th century Khmer Empire were made from unlikely ingredients. Pengyasi was made from the leaves of an unidentified plant, while baolengjiao was made from rice hulls and rice leftovers.

Khmer Empire drinkers in the late 13th century also had a "sugar-shine wine" made from sugar. Another drink, palm starch wine, was made from the starch of the leaves of a palm growing on the riverbank.

art.text: The Khmer Empire ruled from 802 to 1431, and its art is the most famous in Cambodia's history, especially around Angkor. The mainly 12th-century temple complex of Angkor Wat was initially Hindu and subsequently Buddhist.

Between the 13th and 14th centuries, the natives of Banton, Romblon, in the Philippines crafted the Banton cloth. It is the oldest surviving ikat textile in Southeast Asia, and it was used as a death blanket.

Much of the art in Thailand is based on Buddhism. Its first period of art occurred during the Sukhothai Kingdom, which began in the 13th century, and the artworks of that period were mostly drawings of the Buddha.
Balinese art is of Hindu-Javanese origin. It grew from the work of artisans of the Majapahit Kingdom, who expanded to Bali in the late 13th century.
The One Pillar Pagoda in Hanoi was built in 1049, based on a dream of King Lý Thái Tông, who ruled from 1028 to 1054. It is one of the prominent edifices surviving from the feudal era.

Much of the Indian influence on Southeast Asia came in the era of the Chola dynasty. The so-called Indianised Kingdoms adopted, to varying degrees, India's statecraft, administration, art, epigraphy, writing and architecture. They adapted these influences into their own distinct expressions, such as Angkor Wat.

In Brunei, weaving became significant in the 15th century. One example is the Jongsarat, a handmade garment used for weddings and special occasions. It typically includes a hint of silver and gold, and it can also be used for wall coverings.

In 2004, a part of the 900-year-old Hanoi Citadel was discovered in central Hanoi, near the site of Ba Đình Square. Hanoi also hosts the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, which dates back to the Lý dynasty.
The Butuan Silver Paleograph was made between the 12th and 15th centuries in the Philippines. The script on the silver has yet to be deciphered.

war.text: The Mongol Empire and later the Yuan dynasty launched four major campaigns against Đại Việt and Champa in 1258, 1282–1284, 1285, and 1287–1288. Despite suffering major military defeats, the Mongols established tributary relations with Đại Việt. Modern Vietnamese historiography regards the war as a major victory against foreign invaders.

In the 13th century, the Mongols struck Southeast Asia far beyond Vietnam, reaching the Vietnamese coast, inland Burma and Java. The Pagan Kingdom in Burma was invaded from 1277 to 1287, which fragmented it and led to the rise of smaller Shan States ruled by local chieftains.

Elephant duels were a martial practice in which opposing army leaders fought in single combat on the backs of war elephants. They are documented in Southeast Asia, mainly in present-day Cambodia from the 11th century and in Burma and Thailand from the 13th to 16th centuries. Some authors see them as a way to settle a conflict without massive casualties.

In 1258 the Mongol general Uriyangkhadai captured the Vietnamese capital Thăng Long, modern Hanoi. The Mongols found their envoys in prison, one of them already dead, and in revenge massacred the city's inhabitants. After nine days he left to invade the Song dynasty in modern Guangxi in 1259, as part of a coordinated Mongol attack with armies in Sichuan under Möngke Khan and others in Shandong and Henan.

In summer 1282, Kublai ordered Sogetu, the governor of Guangzhou, to lead an expedition against Champa. In late 1282 a Yuan fleet of 5,000 men, 100 ships and 250 landing crafts set sail for the Cham capital. It reached the coast near modern Qui Nhơn in February 1283.

At Thị Nại Bay in February 1283, the Cham defenders marched out of the south gate at 5:00 AM and met the Yuan landing with 10,000 men, several elephants and around 100 Muslim trebuchet. The battle was fiercely fought by both sides, but the Yuan broke the Cham line. Afterward, Chinese troops from the north and east entered the fort and butchered and drowned several thousand of its defenders. King Indravarman V retreated to the western highlands and waged a guerrilla campaign against the occupiers.

In 1292 the Mongols sent envoys to the Singhasari kingdom in Java to demand submission. Singhasari rejected the demand and injured the envoys, so the Mongols sent a large invasion fleet. Singhasari had already collapsed in 1293 after a revolt by its vassal Kadiri.

The Yuan landed at midnight on 13 February 1283 and approached the Cham wooden fortress from three directions. After the Cham defeat, Chinese troops entered the fort and butchered and drowned several thousand of its defenders. The Cham king then set his warehouse on fire and killed the Mongol envoys Yu Yongxian and Yilan before retreating into the mountains. Yuan troops captured Vijaya on 17 February.

When the Mongols reached Java, a local prince named Raden Wijaya offered to help them punish Kadiri. After Kadiri was defeated, Wijaya turned on his Mongol allies. He ambushed their invasion fleet and forced them to leave Java immediately.

Although Đại Việt repelled the Yuan, its capital Thăng Long was razed, many Buddhist sites were decimated, and the Vietnamese suffered major losses in population and property. Famines and starvations ravaged the country from 1290 to 1292, possibly because war led to neglect of water control and men were mobilized away from the rice fields. Trần Nhân Tông rebuilt the Thăng Long citadel in 1291 and 1293.

In 1289 Đại Việt released most Mongol prisoners of war to China. Omar, whose return Kublai particularly demanded, was intentionally drowned when the boat transporting him was contrived to sink. Omar had been taken prisoner at the Battle of Bạch Đằng in 1288.

The earliest mentions of elephant duels in Thailand appear in inscriptions and chronicles of Sukhothai and Lanna from the late 13th century. The practice is believed to have been influenced by the Sri Lankan Buddhist chronicle Mahāvaṃsa, and duels were seen as a heroic deed showing a ruler's prowess and prestige.

literature.text: For most of Vietnam's history, literature was written in Classical Chinese using chữ Hán, the Chinese characters introduced during a thousand years of Chinese rule. From the 13th century, writers also used chữ Nôm, a script that blended Chinese and original Vietnamese characters to write the spoken Vietnamese language.

Vietnamese folk literature was not only an oral tradition but a mixing of three media: hidden, fixed and performed. Only the memory of folk authors kept the hidden form. Such works usually existed in many versions, passed down orally by unknown authors.

The Nôm script let Vietnamese writers create poetic forms such as Lục bát and Song thất lục bát. It also allowed Vietnamese reduplication to be used in poetry. These features made Nôm better suited than Chinese characters to representing Vietnamese literature.

Nguyễn Trãi, who lived from 1380 to 1442, pioneered poetry in Nôm. He wrote Vietnamese verse in Nôm using the Chinese seven-syllable pattern. Only later, in the 17th century, did Vietnamese poetry shift toward a native pattern of alternating six- and eight-syllable lines.

Vietnam's earliest surviving literature by Vietnamese writers is in chữ Hán, including almost all official documents and the first poems. Notable works include imperial proclamations, histories and declarations of independence from China. One example is the Thiên đô chiếu of 1010, an edict moving the capital of Đại Cồ Việt from Hoa Lư to Đại La.

In Vietnam, chữ Nôm adapted Chinese characters to write the vernacular Vietnamese language. Nguyễn Quang Hồng suggests it appeared as early as the 12th century. By the 14th century the predominant spoken language of the elites had shifted from Annamese Middle Chinese toward the ancestor of Vietnamese.

Under the Lê dynasty, which began in 1428, chữ Nôm was banned several times because it was unofficial and was used as a medium for social protest. Even so, a sizable body of Nôm literature had built up by the 19th century. Individuals could spread these texts orally in villages.

Chữ Nôm never replaced chữ Hán as Vietnam's main writing system. Fewer than five percent of educated Vietnamese used it, mostly as a learning aid for chữ Hán and for writing folk literature. Chữ Hán stayed the official administrative script until the 19th century, with two brief exceptions, one under the Hồ dynasty from 1400 to 1407.

In 1060 the Vietnamese emperor Lý Thái Tông ordered a translation of Cham songs. This followed his seaborne raid on Champa in 1044, when Cham women were taken as singers, dancers and entertainers for the court. A special palace for Cham women was built in 1046.

Because chữ Nôm was never standardized, its texts can be ambiguous about which words a writer meant. This led to many variations when Nôm works were transliterated into the modern Vietnamese alphabet.

Chữ Nôm may have been used as early as the 8th century, but concrete textual evidence for it dates only to the 13th century. Texts in Vietnam were written in chữ Hán by the 10th century at the latest.

science.text: Science and technology under the Vietnamese Trần dynasty built on the achievements of the earlier Lý period. It made significant advances in military technology, medicine, astronomy, and calendrical science.

Firearm and cannon technology developed by the Vietnamese proved vital to the conquest of Champa by Đại Việt in the Cham-Vietnamese War of 1471. Vietnamese matchlocks of this period were considered world-class, even by European observers of the Trịnh–Nguyễn civil war.

Chinese traders were sailing to Southeast Asia by the 11th century, though Srivijaya still dominated the trade routes. China's development of its own maritime technologies led to Chinese trading colonies in Southeast Asia and a boom in maritime trade.

In the 15th century the Vietnamese scholar Hồ Nguyên Trừng was known for his innovations on firearms and cannons. While living in exile in China, he helped transfer knowledge of Vietnamese firearm technology.

During the medieval period, the design of Vietnamese armour and helmets took shape, and it was depicted in sculptures and reliefs preserved in temples. In naval warfare, the Vietnamese developed the Mông đồng, a type of warship used by their naval forces.

In Vietnamese mechanical engineering, machines were used in production but were also designed for ceremonial and spiritual activities. According to the Sùng Thiện Diên Linh stele, Emperor Lý Nhân Tông (1066–1128) ordered the construction of the Quảng Chiếu lantern pavilion.

politics.text: The Lý dynasty was founded in 1009 when Lý Công Uẩn overthrew the Anterior Lê dynasty. It lasted 216 years. In 1225 the eight-year-old empress Lý Chiêu Hoàng was pressured to abdicate in favor of her husband, Trần Cảnh. The article adds that the former emperor Huệ Tông was forced to commit suicide at Chân Giáo Temple, and that Trần Thủ Độ had the Lý aristocrats massacred in 1232.

The Chola Empire, based in southern India, was a thalassocratic empire with dominions and spheres of influence in Southeast Asia. Its power was shown in naval raids on cities of the Srivijaya Empire on Sumatra and in repeated embassies to China. Around 1070 it began to lose almost all its overseas territories.

Srivijaya was a thalassocratic empire that emerged by the 7th century by conquering neighboring maritime states. It controlled the sea lanes in Southeast Asia and the trade routes between India and China. Singhasari subjugated it around 1275, and it was later absorbed by Majapahit, which lasted from 1293 to 1527.

The Angkor empire flourished from the 9th to the early 13th century. It peaked under Jayavarman VII at the end of the 12th century, when its conquests reached into Thailand in the west, where it conquered the Mon kingdom of Dwaravati, and into Champa in the east.
politics.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia

politics.text: Hanoi's Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu) is the site of the oldest university in Vietnam, which was started in 1010. That was the same year Emperor Lý Thái Tổ founded the capital Thăng Long, meaning 'ascending dragon'.
Under Lý Thánh Tông, the state's official name changed from Đại Cồ Việt to Đại Việt in 1054. That name stayed Vietnam's official name until the onset of the 19th century.

The Lý court built a state run on examinations. The Temple of Literature opened in 1070, the first imperial examination was held in 1075, and in 1089 a fixed hierarchy of officials with nine degrees was established. Examinations for public office became compulsory.

In the 10th century Mataram challenged the supremacy of Srivijaya, and in response Srivijaya destroyed the Mataram capital early in the 11th century. King Airlangga (c. 1020–1050) restored the kingdom, but it split on his death, and the new state of Kediri was formed in eastern Java.
politics.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia

politics.text: Anawrahta, ruler of the Pagan Empire in Burma, is considered the founder of the modern Burmese nation. He revived the Mon people's form of Theravada Buddhism by building schools and monasteries. His success later helped Buddhism revive and grow in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. The article also notes that Buddhist kings of the time, to maintain their power and purify the faith, tried to unify Buddhist sects by eliminating heretical movements, meeting resistance from the cult of Nat worship.

In 1075 the Song chancellor Wang Anshi told Emperor Shenzong that Đại Việt had been destroyed by Champa, with fewer than ten thousand soldiers surviving, and should be annexed. Instead, Lý Thường Kiệt led a preemptive invasion of Song territory, capturing Qinzhou and Lianzhou and besieging Yongzhou. Yongzhou fell in 1076, and its population of 58,000 was massacred. The Song later returned the conquered lands and recognized Lý Nhân Tông as King of Nam Bình.

In 1025 the Chola ruler Rajendra Chola successfully invaded cities of Srivijaya in Malaysia and Indonesia. The invasion failed to install direct administration, because it was short and meant only to plunder Srivijaya's wealth.

The naval expeditions of Zheng He between 1405 and 1431 also played a critical role in opening China to increased trade with Southeast Asian polities. Trade with China ceased after the collapse of the Song dynasty due to invasions and famine. It was restored during the Ming dynasty, from the 14th to 16th centuries.

philosophy.text: Before the 14th century, Hinduism and Buddhism were the dominant religions of Southeast Asia. Thereafter, Islam became dominant in Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei.

Anawrahta (1014–1077) ruled the Pagan Empire in Burma and revived the Mon people's form of Theravada Buddhism. He built schools and monasteries that taught and supported Theravada ideologies. His success later allowed Buddhism to revive and grow in Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia.

The first Muslim inscriptions in Southeast Asia date to the 11th century. One from 1028 was found in Pahang, Malaysia, an Arabic pillar inscription from between 1029 and 1035 in Champa, and an Arabic engraving from 1048 in Brunei marking a Muslim woman's tomb.

The middle of the 11th century saw a decline of Buddhism in Southeast Asia. From the 11th to 13th century the Khmer Empire dominated the peninsula. Hinduism was its primary religion, with a smaller portion of people adhering to Mahayana Buddhism.

When Ibn Batutta visited Samudra Pasai in 1345, he noted that people in the ports were Muslim but those in the interior were 'pagans'. This showed a dual situation: cosmopolitan ports were largely Muslim, while the vast hinterland was not.
The Lý dynasty of 11th-century Vietnam was deeply influenced by Buddhism. In 1031, the reigning monarch Lý Thái Tông had 950 pagodas constructed.

Hindu-Buddhist influences were incorporated into Southeast Asian political systems. The Angkor empire flourished from the 9th to the early 13th century, peaking under Jayavarman VII at the end of the 12th century. Its most celebrated memorial is the great temple of Angkor Wat, built early in the 12th century.
philosophy.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia

philosophy.text: During the classical era of the Khmer Empire, administration, agriculture, architecture, hydrology, urban planning, literature and the arts reached an unprecedented degree of development. The source credits this to the distinct expression of Hindu cosmology. Ideas about the universe shaped how the kingdom was built and run.
Chinese sources record a Muslim delegation from the Kingdom of Samudra (Pasai) to the emperor in 1282. When Marco Polo visited in 1292, he noted that the urban port state of Perlak was Muslim.

Two Kufic gravestones found in Phan Rang, dating from 1038 to 1039, mark an Arab Muslim merchant named Abu Kamil, who came from Egypt. They indicate a certain autonomy for a Muslim merchant community in Panduranga, granted by a Cham king who understood their importance to trade.

The kingdoms of Champa controlled what is now south and central Vietnam, and their dominant religion was Hinduism. By the late fifteenth century, the Vietnamese had eradicated the last traces of Champa. The last surviving Chams began their diaspora in 1471.
The legendary king of Panduranga, Po Ovlvah, reigned from 1000 to 1036 in the Cham annals. His name is believed to be a Cham rendition of Allah.

Al-Dimashqi claimed that after being expelled, a small portion of Alids took refuge in Champa. These Muslim immigrants supposedly spread Shi'a among the Cham, which perhaps eventually led to the synthesis of the Bani Awal religion.

culture.text: For centuries Southeast Asia lay within India's cultural sphere, as Hindu-Buddhist influences were built into local political systems. Rulers used these ideas to gain power and stability, turning small chieftains into regional powers. This influence lasted until the 15th century CE.
culture.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia

culture.text: Southeast Asians played a board game using boat-shaped wooden boards with cup-shaped holes. It is known as congkak in Malaysia, congklak or dakon in Indonesia, and sungkâ in the Philippines. Players sow seeds, usually small cowrie shells, pebbles or tamarind seeds, around the holes.

Angkor Wat, the most celebrated memorial of the Angkor empire, was built early in the 12th century. The empire flourished from the 9th to the early 13th century and reached the peak of its fame under Jayavarman VII at the end of the 12th century. Its conquests then extended into Thailand and Champa.
culture.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia

culture.text: The Old Javanese poem Deśavarṇana, completed in 1365, describes vassal states of the Majapahit Empire spread throughout much of today's Indonesia. This made Majapahit possibly the largest empire ever to exist in Southeast Asia, though the true character of its control is unclear. The empire declined in the early 16th century as Islamic states rose on coastal Java, the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra.

Hokkien merchants settled among Southeast Asian polities and, without the Chinese government's sanction, built business and trade networks between cities such as Melaka, Hội An and Ayutthaya. Many integrated into their new countries, becoming political officials and diplomats. They helped spread cultural exchange with Southeast Asia.

In Southeast Asian mancala, players in Malaysia call the holes lubang and the larger store holes rumah, meaning house. In Indonesia the holes are anak, meaning child, and the stores are indung, meaning mother. In the Philippines the store hole is called ulo, meaning head.

In the 13th-century Chinese work Zhu Fan Zhi, the island of Timor is called Ti-wu and noted for its sandalwood. Writing towards 1350, Wang Dayuan refers to a Ku-li Ti-men, a corruption of Giri Timor. Giri comes from the Sanskrit word for mountain, so the name means mountainous island of Timor.
culture.source_title: History of Indian influence on Southeast Asia
